The post 13 Best Agent Gateways in 2026 for MCP, A2A and LLM Traffic: Kong, Bifrost, AgentCore, Arcade appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Agents no longer just call a model. They call tools over MCP, delegate to other agents over A2A, and act inside business systems. The best agent gateways sit on that path and decide who can do what. This list compares 13 of them on traffic coverage, identity, deployment and price. What is an agent gateway? An agent gateway is a control point that authenticates agents, filters the tools they see, and logs every call. A plain LLM gateway only routes model requests. An agent gateway adds MCP tool governance, agent identity and, increasingly, A2A traffic control. Our ranking below is editorial and weighs 5 criteria: traffic coverage, identity and authorization, deployment options, maturity, and price transparency. How the 13 best agent gateways rank 1. Kong AI Gateway Kong governs LLM, MCP and A2A traffic from 1 control plane. Version 2.0 moved AI features into first-class Providers, Models, MCP Servers and Agents entities . Best for: teams already running Kong for API management. Watch out: the 2.x architecture needs a Konnect control plane. Arcade notes the MCP OAuth2 plugin is still Tech Preview. 2. Bifrost (Maxim AI) Bifrost is an Apache 2.0 Go gateway covering models, MCP tools and A2A agents in 1 deployment. Maxim reports 10,000+ models across 25+ providers. Its benchmark claims 11 µs mean overhead at 5,000 RPS . Best for: self-hosted, in-VPC or air-gapped teams that want all 3 traffic types. Watch out: SSO, SCIM and token exchange are Enterprise-only. An independent review notes the 11 µs figure excludes HTTP handling and JSON marshalling. 3. Gravitee AI Gateway Gravitee runs an LLM Proxy, MCP Proxy and A2A Proxy on 1 runtime. All 3 share 1 authentication, policy and OpenTelemetry chain. The A2A Proxy supports RFC 8693 token exchange and skill-level authorization. Best for: enterprises that want agent identity modeled alongside existing APIs. Watch out: Maxim lists Agent Management from $2,500 per month. The A2A Proxy needs Enterprise Edition. 4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway AgentCore Gateway gives agents 1 managed endpoint for tools, models and other agents . It adds semantic tool search, Cedar policies and on-behalf-of token exchange. Pricing starts at $0.005 per 1,000 invocations . Best for: AWS-native teams using IAM, CloudWatch and Bedrock Guardrails. Watch out: AWS-only. A2A is HTTP passthrough, per Maxim . Search calls cost $0.025 per 1,000 , 5x the invoke rate. 5. Arcade.dev Arcade is an actions runtime, not a model router. Per Arcade , it checks the overlap of user and agent permissions on every action. Credentials never reach the LLM. It lists 8,000+ agent-optimized tools. Best for: agents that write to Salesforce, Gmail or Slack on a user’s behalf. Watch out: no model routing, so pair it with an LLM gateway. Pricing is $25 per month plus $0.10 per auth event and $0.01 per tool call. 6. Prisma AIRS AI Gateway (formerly Portkey) Palo Alto Networks completed its Portkey acquisition in May 2026. The gateway reached GA inside Prisma AIRS in July 2026. Palo Alto describes it as a unified LLM, MCP and A2A gateway with 1 enforcement point. It runs in SaaS and hybrid models . Best for: security teams that want runtime inspection on every prompt. Watch out: pricing is not public. Arcade advises verifying delegated auth and audit depth for agent actions. 7. Azure API Management Microsoft’s AI gateway extends API Management to model APIs, MCP servers and A2A agent APIs. It can expose REST APIs as MCP servers and front existing MCP servers. Best for: Microsoft-centric API teams. Watch out: A2A support is preview, JSON-RPC only, and limited to v2 tiers. 8. Google Cloud Agent Gateway Agent Gateway is the network entry and exit point for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It assigns each agent a SPIFFE ID and can apply Model Armor to prompts and responses. Maxim lists up to 5,000 governed resources per gateway. Best for: teams building on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Watch out: Maxim reports cross-cloud support as “coming soon.” Model routing and fallback are not documented. 9. IBM ContextForge ContextForge is an Apache 2.0 registry and proxy that federates MCP, REST, gRPC and A2A. It exposes agents as MCP tools and, per Maxim , deploys via Helm. Best for: free, MCP-first, self-hosted Kubernetes setups. Watch out: no published commercial support. IBM recommends upgrading to v1.1.1 after security bulletins covering v1.0.0 to v1.1.0. 10. Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) Envoy AI Gateway became Agent Router and joined the Agentic AI Foundation in September 2026. It offers an OpenAI-compatible API plus an MCP gateway on Envoy. Best for: Kubernetes teams already on Envoy Gateway. Watch out: A2A is preview and JSON-RPC only. Maxim notes no built-in guardrails. 11. Composio Composio is an MCP gateway and SaaS integration layer with managed OAuth and per-user connected accounts. Arcade lists a free tier of 100,000 tool calls per month and Pro from $29. Best for: fast access to a large prebuilt SaaS catalog. Watch out: Arcade notes sessions are discoverable by default unless allowlisted. 12. TrueFoundry TrueFoundry combines an LLM Gateway and centralized MCP access with training and deployment tooling. Pro costs $25 per user per month , with 20,000 requests and tool calls per user. Best for: ML teams that want gateway and MLOps in 1 platform. Watch out: the client-credentials MCP flow uses a shared identity, not the user’s, Arcade notes . 13. Obot Obot is an open-source platform bundling an MCP Gateway, LLM Gateway and device monitoring. It supports per-user auth, OAuth token exchange and audit logs. Best for: IT teams rolling out MCP servers to employees. Watch out: self-hosting alone does not settle downstream authorization, Arcade notes . Optimized prompts score 56.0 versus 44.6 for the best hand-written harness on Continual Learning Bench. The post Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory , a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. TL;DR Method: The base is Kimi-K2.6 , a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active and 256K context. Distillation adds a LoRA adapter (rank 64) on attention projections. Runs on: Training hardware is not disclosed. Kimi-K2.6 serving needs a multi-GPU node; Vast.ai recommends 8x H200 . Native INT4 weights exist. Performance: Self-found memory prompts average 56.0 on 3 tasks, versus 44.6 for the best human-written ones. Best: Codebase, 64.3 with optimized prompts, +20.6 over the best hand-written harness. Worst: Spectrum distillation adds only 2.9 points (46.5 vs 43.6 for SFT on generic runs). What is Self-Improving Memory? Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. How does harness optimization work? In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. Each candidate runs the full task stream 5 times. The top 4 by mean score become parents for revision. For each parent, the meta agent reads trajectories, scores and final memory directories. It then proposes revised prompts. Selection uses a holdout set the meta agent cannot see. The discovered prompts are concrete. One Database prompt says to read GUARDRAILS.md, then SCHEMA.md, before answering. The best Codebase design uses a quickstart file, an indexed fix registry and separate fix files. How does harness distillation move the gains into weights? Stage 2 follows a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline. The task agent runs train subtasks with the optimized prompts. Every model call is logged. The research team then swaps the optimized prompts back to the generic ones in that history. The swap works because the behavior stays valid under generic instructions. Examples include keeping QUICKSTART.md, REGISTRY.md and SCHEMA.md files, and verifying join keys before aggregation. The model is fine-tuned with LoRA, rank 64, on attention projection layers. The loss covers only assistant tokens, including reasoning and tool calls. Each task gets equal weight. The meta agent and task agent are the same Kimi-K2.6 model. So the model is trained on memory skills it discovered itself. What do the benchmarks show? The tests use 3 Continual Learning Bench tasks: Database (SQL), Codebase (repo fixes) and Spectrum (radio scans). Test subtasks follow a designed phase shift. So results measure generalization to new instances of the same tasks. Test score Database Codebase Spectrum Average No memory 7.5 31.8 21.9 20.4 Compaction 39.8 36.9 34.6 37.1 Generic harness 32.3 33.5 42.5 36.1 Best human-written 47.9 43.7 42.1 44.6 Optimized harness 53.8 64.3 49.9 56.0 SFT on generic trajectories 31.6 37.5 43.6 37.6 SFT on optimized trajectories (generic prompts) 37.7 45.1 46.5 43.1 Source: Figures 4 and 5, Self-Improving Memory blog . Kimi-K2.6 for all rows. Optimized harnesses beat the best hand-written seed on all 3 tasks. Codebase gained the most, at 20.6 points. Search was noisy: 37 of 44 generated revisions failed to beat the previous best. Database and Spectrum peaked in the first generation. Codebase kept improving through generation 4. After distillation, every model runs the generic harness. The distilled model averages 43.1 across 10 matched seeds. SFT on generic trajectories reaches 37.6. That is a 5.5-point gain, or 14.6%. How does it compare with ALMA, MemEvolve and Harness-Zero? Several recent methods search over agent memory or harnesses. Self-Improving Memory searches memory prompts, then distills them into weights. Benchmarks differ, so headline numbers are not directly comparable. Feature Self-Improving Memory ALMA MemEvolve Harness-Zero Org FAIR at Meta, UW, JHU Xiong, Hu, Clune OPPO AI Agent Team, LV-NUS Peking University, Google, HKUST What is searched LOAD/OFFLOAD memory prompts Memory designs as Python code Memory architecture and contents Full agent harness Trains weights Yes, LoRA rank 64 No No Yes, LoRA SFT Models Kimi-K2.6 (agent and meta agent) GPT-5 meta agent, GPT-5-nano/mini task agent GPT-5-mini (plus DeepSeek V3.2, Kimi K2) Qwen3.5-9B student Benchmarks Continual Learning Bench (3 tasks) ALFWorld, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack GAIA, WebWalkerQA, xBench-DeepSearch, TaskCraft SpreadsheetBench Verified, AppWorld, USPTO Retrosynthesis Headline result 56.0 vs 44.6 best human harness; 43.1 distilled 53.9% vs 41.1% no memory (GPT-5-mini) Up to 17.06% gains 23.3% to 44.3% with harness removed Code Not released GitHub GitHub GitHub Harness-Zero is the closest match, but it uses a separate agent to correct the student. Self-Improving Memory skips that step. Key Takeaways Kimi-K2.6 writes memory prompts that beat human ones: 56.0 vs 44.6. Codebase sees the biggest jump: 64.3, up 20.6 points. Distillation keeps part of the gain: 43.1 vs 37.6 with generic prompts. 37 of 44 meta-agent revisions failed, so evaluation and selection matter. Every day, hosts offer unique stays and experiences that make it possible for guests to connect with communities in a more authentic way.</span></p></div><h1><strong>Senior Data Engineer, Enterprise Core Datasets, Tech Foundations</strong></h1> <h3><strong>The Community You Will Join</strong></h3> <p>At Airbnb, trustworthy data powers business decisions, product innovation, and operational efficiency. The Enterprise Core Datasets team builds the technical data foundations that help Airbnb understand how the business operates, where resources are invested, and how new technologies create value.</p> <p>Our scope spans high-impact datasets across the organization: measuring AI adoption, usage, and cost; understanding revenue, costs, and profitability through Unit Economics; integrating non-platform data from Jira and other enterprise applications; and powering critical company metrics such as Gross Booking Value and Revenue.</p> <p>You will join a team that values thoughtful architecture, engineering rigor, and operational ownership. We collaborate with engineering, product, analytics, finance, and business teams to turn complex requirements into dependable, reusable data assets. We welcome strong engineers who are curious about the business and eager to solve problems across diverse domains.</p> <h3><strong>The Difference You Will Make</strong></h3> <p>As a Senior Data Engineer, you will design, build, and operate datasets that shape decisions across Airbnb. Your work will help the organization measure AI adoption and spending, understand the economics of its products, and connect enterprise application data to meaningful business and operational insights.</p> <p>You will own complex data engineering projects from requirements gathering and technical design through implementation, validation, and production operations. Working closely with stakeholders and engineering partners, you will build maintainable data models and pipelines that accommodate new AI tools, products, cost categories, and enterprise systems while preserving clear definitions, traceability, and reliable historical data.</p> <p>Operating in an ecosystem that includes petabyte-scale datasets, you will improve correctness, freshness, performance, and cost efficiency. You will build reusable components that simplify source onboarding and reduce duplicated logic. Through design reviews, knowledge sharing, and mentorship, you will help strengthen the team’s engineering practices and contribute to Airbnb’s broader data community.</p> <h3><strong>A Typical Day</strong></h3> <ul> <li>Design, build, and operate high-impact data pipelines across AI usage and cost, Unit Economics, enterprise applications, and critical financial metrics.</li> <li>Partner with stakeholders to clarify how AI adoption, consumption, and spending are measured, and implement consistent data models that support those definitions.</li> <li>Evolve Unit Economics datasets to connect revenue and diverse cost drivers, enabling teams to understand product profitability and resource efficiency.</li> <li>Build reliable ingestion and transformation pipelines for non-platform systems such as Jira and other BizTech enterprise applications.</li> <li>Translate complex requirements into clear source contracts, reusable fact and dimension models, and practical technical designs.</li> <li>Develop configurable pipelines and shared components that simplify onboarding new data sources, products, and business requirements.</li> <li>Implement automated testing, reconciliation, anomaly detection, and monitoring to protect data accuracy, completeness, and availability.</li> <li>Plan and execute safe migrations and historical backfills through dependency analysis, validation, controlled cutovers, and recovery planning.</li> <li>Optimize distributed processing, storage, and query performance to improve freshness and reduce compute costs.</li> <li>Own production reliability for your datasets and pipelines through on-call participation, incident response, and improvements to systems and runbooks.</li> <li>Contribute to technical planning and design reviews, mentor fellow engineers, and improve Airbnb’s Data Engineering Paved Path.</li> </ul> <h3><strong>Your Expertise</strong></h3> <ul> <li>5+ years of relevant industry experience, with a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, or a related field, or equivalent practical experience.</li> <li>A track record of independently delivering complex data engineering projects, from requirements and technical design through implementation and sustained production ownership.</li> <li>Strong expertise in SQL and programming skills in Python or Scala, with experience building maintainable, well-tested data systems.</li> <li>Hands-on experience with distributed processing technologies such as Apache Spark and large-scale analytical storage systems.</li> <li>Strong data modeling skills, including fact and dimension design, slowly changing dimensions, incremental processing, and historical data management.</li> <li>Experience integrating heterogeneous sources, including APIs, enterprise applications, event data, and transactional systems, while managing schema changes and source reliability.</li> <li>Proven ability to build reliable pipelines and execute migrations and backfills while preserving correctness and downstream compatibility.</li> <li>Experience implementing data quality controls, observability, lineage, and governance practices, and troubleshooting production data issues.</li> <li>The ability to diagnose performance bottlenecks and optimize distributed computation, storage, and query execution.</li> <li>Strong collaboration and communication skills, including the ability to clarify requirements with business partners, explain technical tradeoffs, and coordinate delivery across teams.</li> <li>Experience contributing to design and code reviews, sharing knowledge, and supporting the development of other engineers.</li> <li>Curiosity and sound judgment when learning new domains and balancing delivery needs with long-term system health.</li> </ul> <p>Experience with AI usage or cost measurement, cloud cost attribution, Unit Economics, enterprise application data, or financial and payments datasets is a plus. Familiarity with workflow orchestration, SQL transformation frameworks, and modern table formats such as Apache Iceberg is also valuable.</p> <h3><strong>Your Location</strong></h3> <p>This position is US - Remote Eligible. The role may include occasional work at an Airbnb office or attendance at offsites, as agreed to with your manager. While the position is Remote Eligible, you must live in a state where Airbnb, Inc. has a registered entity. Click here for the up-to-date list of exclude

Fin can also be combined with our natively integrated Intercom help desk, giving modern support teams one single system.</p> <p>Together with Salesforce, the #1 AI CRM, where humans with agents drive customer success, we're building the future of customer experience. You're in the right place. This role will shape how we engage with large, complex organizations, defining our go-to-market, building a world-class team, and delivering tangible customer outcomes through innovation and credibility.</p> <p>This role is both strategic and hands-on. You will lead a Solutions Engineering team focused on winning complex deals, creating vertical-specific solution architectures, and building repeatable playbooks. We believe in leaders who are open to be a player and a coach, regardless of seniority. You’ll collaborate closely with Sales, Success, Product, Engineering, and Services to deliver customer transformation through Intercom’s AI-first platform – be it through strategic guidance as a senior leader on the team, or securing deals with your own technical credibility where needed.</p> <h2>What will I be doing?&nbsp;</h2> <ul> <li>Define and evolve the strategic vision and go-to-market (GTM) approach for the Solutions Engineering function.</li> <li>Lead, coach, and scale a high-performing SE team across global regions and core verticals.</li> <li>Operate as a player-coach, actively engaging in strategic deals while developing team capabilities.</li> <li>Support complex, six-figure sales cycles with technical guidance, architecture, demos, and product evaluation support, as well as sales expertise.</li> <li>Serve as a trusted technical advisor and executive point of contact for large customers.</li> <li>Partner closely with Sales, Product, Marketing, and R&amp;D to shape verticalized GTM motions and solution strategy.</li> <li>Champion a customer-obsessed culture across the pre-sales journey – from outbound to implementation.</li> <li>Lead discovery, design, and delivery of tailored technical solutions, including PoCs and business value assessments.</li> <li>Build reusable, scalable solution frameworks, and industry-specific technical assets.</li> <li>Advocate for customer needs and insights internally to influence product roadmap and prioritization.</li> <li>Represent Intercom and the SE function externally through executive meetings and strategic events.</li> <li>Foster strong relationships with C-level stakeholders, translating AI product capabilities into tangible business impact.</li> </ul> <h2>What skills do I need?&nbsp;</h2> <ul> <li>5+ years of pre-sales experience as a Sales Engineer, Solutions Engineer/Architect, or related individual contributor role.</li> <li>Having 3+ years of experience leading technical pre-sales teams, with a proven track record of hiring, mentoring, and managing high-performing teams.</li> <li>Ideally, experience selling AI, data, or highly technical products; or at the very least, deep curiosity and utilization of AI on your day-to-day.</li> <li>Comfortable with ambiguity in environments with an ability to stay focused and thrive under pressure while working with customers to solve their most challenging issues.</li> <li>Have a humble attitude, and a passion to help others, with a willingness to learn whatever it takes to support the team and help our customers thrive.</li> <li>A track record of consistently delivering revenue numbers, producing accurate forecasts, while maintaining a focus on team development and growth</li> <li>Excellent communication and presentation skills</li> </ul> <p>The OTE salary range for candidates within the San Francisco Bay Area or NYC is $279,000-$333,250. Actual base pay will depend on a variety of factors such as education, skills, experience, location, etc. The base pay range is subject to change and may be modified in the future. All regular employees may also be eligible for the corporate bonus program or a sales incentive (target included in OTE) as well as stock in the form of Restricted Stock Units (RSUs).&nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p>#LI-Hybrid</p><div class="content-conclusion"><p><strong>Unleash Your Potential</strong></p> <p>When you join Salesforce, you’ll be limitless in all areas of your life. Our benefits and resources support you to find balance and be your best, and our AI agents accelerate your impact so you can do your best. Together, we’ll bring the power of Agentforce to organizations of all sizes and deliver amazing experiences that customers love. Apply today to not only shape the future — but to redefine what’s possible — for yourself, for AI, and the world.</p> <p>In the United States, compensation offered will be determined by factors such as location, job level, job-related knowledge, skills, and experience. Certain roles may be eligible for incentive compensation, equity, and benefits. At Fin, we want to give people what they need to do the best work of their careers. Our benefits and programs are designed to support your health and wellbeing, your family, your time away from work, and your financial future. Offerings vary by location in line with local practices and requirements. Learn more about working at Fin and the benefits we offer at<a href="http://fin.ai/careers"> fin.ai/careers</a>. Optimized prompts score 56.0 versus 44.6 for the best hand-written harness on Continual Learning Bench. The post Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory , a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. TL;DR Method: The base is Kimi-K2.6 , a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active and 256K context. Distillation adds a LoRA adapter (rank 64) on attention projections. Runs on: Training hardware is not disclosed. Kimi-K2.6 serving needs a multi-GPU node; Vast.ai recommends 8x H200 . Native INT4 weights exist. Performance: Self-found memory prompts average 56.0 on 3 tasks, versus 44.6 for the best human-written ones. Best: Codebase, 64.3 with optimized prompts, +20.6 over the best hand-written harness. Worst: Spectrum distillation adds only 2.9 points (46.5 vs 43.6 for SFT on generic runs). What is Self-Improving Memory? Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. How does harness optimization work? In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. Each candidate runs the full task stream 5 times. The top 4 by mean score become parents for revision. For each parent, the meta agent reads trajectories, scores and final memory directories. It then proposes revised prompts. Selection uses a holdout set the meta agent cannot see. The discovered prompts are concrete. One Database prompt says to read GUARDRAILS.md, then SCHEMA.md, before answering. The best Codebase design uses a quickstart file, an indexed fix registry and separate fix files. How does harness distillation move the gains into weights? Stage 2 follows a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline. The task agent runs train subtasks with the optimized prompts. Every model call is logged. The research team then swaps the optimized prompts back to the generic ones in that history. The swap works because the behavior stays valid under generic instructions. Examples include keeping QUICKSTART.md, REGISTRY.md and SCHEMA.md files, and verifying join keys before aggregation. The model is fine-tuned with LoRA, rank 64, on attention projection layers. The loss covers only assistant tokens, including reasoning and tool calls. Each task gets equal weight. The meta agent and task agent are the same Kimi-K2.6 model. So the model is trained on memory skills it discovered itself. What do the benchmarks show? The tests use 3 Continual Learning Bench tasks: Database (SQL), Codebase (repo fixes) and Spectrum (radio scans). Test subtasks follow a designed phase shift. So results measure generalization to new instances of the same tasks. Test score Database Codebase Spectrum Average No memory 7.5 31.8 21.9 20.4 Compaction 39.8 36.9 34.6 37.1 Generic harness 32.3 33.5 42.5 36.1 Best human-written 47.9 43.7 42.1 44.6 Optimized harness 53.8 64.3 49.9 56.0 SFT on generic trajectories 31.6 37.5 43.6 37.6 SFT on optimized trajectories (generic prompts) 37.7 45.1 46.5 43.1 Source: Figures 4 and 5, Self-Improving Memory blog . Kimi-K2.6 for all rows. Optimized harnesses beat the best hand-written seed on all 3 tasks. Codebase gained the most, at 20.6 points. Search was noisy: 37 of 44 generated revisions failed to beat the previous best. Database and Spectrum peaked in the first generation. Codebase kept improving through generation 4. After distillation, every model runs the generic harness. The distilled model averages 43.1 across 10 matched seeds. SFT on generic trajectories reaches 37.6. That is a 5.5-point gain, or 14.6%. How does it compare with ALMA, MemEvolve and Harness-Zero? Several recent methods search over agent memory or harnesses. Self-Improving Memory searches memory prompts, then distills them into weights. Benchmarks differ, so headline numbers are not directly comparable. It more than doubles Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 to 12.0 and runs on a single GPU. The post RadixArk Ships DaisyRose-27B, a 27B Agentic Coding Model Trained With Reinforcement Learning Only appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> This week RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B , its first open-weight model. DaisyRose-27B is an agentic coding model from RadixArk, post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning (RL). The model card page states that it used RL only, with no SFT or distillation. It ships under Apache 2.0 as a drop-in replacement for the base model. The main result: Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 rises from 5.6 to 12.0. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 27.8B dense parameters (0.46B vision encoder, 0.42B MTP head), 262,144-token context. Runs on: 1 GPU. BF16 is about 52 GB, FP8 about 29 GB, NVFP4 about 23 GB (Blackwell only). Listed targets: H200, B200, GB300, RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090, DGX Spark. GGUF also available. Performance: Beats its Qwen3.8-27B base on all 7 reported benchmarks. Best: IFBench 82.4, the top score among the 9 models RadixArk compared. Worst: HLE (text only) 34.3, only +0.4 over the base and below Inkling 2 Small’s 44.1. Bottom line: Best: Terminal Bench 4.1 more than doubles after 18 days of RL. Worst: it still trails much larger MoE models on hard agentic tasks. What is DaisyRose-27B? DaisyRose-27B keeps the Qwen3.8-27B architecture unchanged. The model card lists 64 decoder layers in a 3:1 pattern. Three Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers alternate with 1 full-attention layer. Hidden size is 5,120. A 27-layer vision encoder handles images. One multi-token-prediction layer supports speculative decoding. Input is text and images, output is text, and it is a thinking model. How was DaisyRose-27B trained? RadixArk built about 1,200 curated tasks with Eigent AI , chosen from thousands of candidates. Each task targets a specific failure of the base model. Each sandbox attempt allows up to 1.5 hours, 100+ tool calls and 256k+ output tokens. Agent sessions reach up to 1M tokens, per the blog . Training ran on Miles , RadixArk’s open-source RL framework, in fully asynchronous mode. The run used 144 H200 GPUs for 18 days. Of those, 128 handled agent inference and 16 handled training. Total compute was 63,000 GPU-hours. RadixArk reports 37% MFU on its internal backend. An open-source Megatron-based trainer reached 16%. End-to-end throughput was 16.8k tokens/s versus 8.3k, a 2.0x speedup. RadixArk says this cut GPU time by 57%. Sandboxes ran on AgentENV . RadixArk reports about 944,000 sandboxes from mid-September to mid-November. Peak concurrency hit 1,566. Creation success was 99% over 9 weeks. RadixArk puts the cost about 80% below popular cloud sandbox providers. How does DaisyRose-27B perform on benchmarks? All scores are self-reported by RadixArk. DaisyRose scores are the higher of its BF16 and FP8 runs. Benchmark DaisyRose-27B Qwen3.8-27B Change Terminal Bench 4.1 (pass@1) 12.0 5.6 +6.4 Terminal Bench 2.1 75.5 73.0 +2.5 DeepSWE v1.1 46.2 42.2 +4.0 SWE Bench Pro v2 94.7 91.3 +3.4 HLE (text only) 34.3 33.9 +0.4 IFBench 82.4 79.5 +2.9 GPQA Diamond 90.7 89.2 +1.5 Source: RadixArk blog and model card . The largest jump is Terminal Bench 4.1, which more than doubles. Coding gains are steady: +4.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and +3.4 on SWE Bench Pro v2. Knowledge gains are small, at +0.4 on HLE and +1.5 on GPQA Diamond. Against larger models, results are mixed. MiMo V2.6 Flash (309B total) leads Terminal Bench 4.1 at 16.1. Inkling 2 Small (594B total) leads DeepSWE at 72.1 and HLE at 44.1. DaisyRose-27B tops RadixArk’s 9-model table only on IFBench. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 19 Nov 2026 21:10:30 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.13 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 The Blue Economy: The World’s Quietest Economic Engine And Its Smartest Cities https://news.crunchbase.com/startups/blue-economy-technology-defense-energy-onetti-mind-the-bridge/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:00:45 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94402 By Alberto Onetti The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy. For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources. Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central. Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea. Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge ’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge. Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end. The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end. The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026). Not all blue tech is the same Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups. We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density). The result is a matrix highlighting: Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total). High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech. The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies. Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’ The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy? Short answer: ports. Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy. And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook. To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation. While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy. The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy. To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units. Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges. Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona , a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge . Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them. Get the full story in Mind The Bridge’s report, available for free download here . Alberto Onetti is chairman of Mind the Bridge and a professor at University of Insubria . He is a serial entrepreneur who has started three startups in his career, the last of which is Funambol , among the five Italian scaleups that have raised the largest amount of capital. He is recognized among the leading international experts in open innovation and has wide experience in setting up and managing open innovation projects — venture clients, venture builders, intrapreneurship, CVCs — with large multinational companies, as well as advising and training on this subject. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 19 Nov 2026 21:10:30 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.13 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Reflecting Sunlight From Space, Better Breathing And Smarter Garbage Trucks https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/interesting-startup-deals-ai-solar-healthcare-space-tech/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:00:25 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94408 This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here . What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car? Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a company bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look. $73.5M to reflect sunlight from space Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down. To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset. The company recently announced $73.5 million in new funding , bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase . Existing investors Sequoia Capital , Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures , Convective Capital , The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1 . Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be launched aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark. The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships. The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally , per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records. Related Crunchbase queries: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding Global Cleantech Startup Funding In 2026 $62M to make better breathing a bigger business Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade. The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness company recently announced a $62 million investment from Camino Partners , the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky . Intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward. The company markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It says it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years. Intake plans to use the new capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful. Its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026 , putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows. Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software. Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026 $12M to bring AI to the garbage-hauling business Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated. San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana , with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital , Harlem Capital and CreativeCo . The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets. TrashLab says its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection. The company says hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform. It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot , a London-based company using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there. Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler. The startup recently announced a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures , with participation from Y Combinator , Thin Line Capital , Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor . Neuron is developing a new kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language. Its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get new production lines up and running. The startup says it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It plans to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.
